note: A documentation refresh run as two passes over the current tree — drift reconciliation (every checkable README/docs claim vs shipped code) and a fresh adversarial standup in the tradition of FINDINGS-2026-08-05-docs-standup.md, recorded in FINDINGS-2026-08-10-docs-refresh.md. The 08-05 audit's findings were all confirmed fixed by execution. What remained clustered in the one part of the project-layout tree that had no gate, plus a marquee feature (the browser-held key) and a new demo that shipped ahead of their README lines. The decisions below are the three worth keeping: how the recurring layout drift was closed for good, the one code change this pass first deferred and then shipped when the operator asked for it, and the one measurement deliberately left as written.

decisions.question: The nestor/*.py layout tree is gated exact and stayed clean; the docs/ and root portion had no gate and drifted twice (FINDINGS-2026-08-05 §8, again on 08-10 — seven docs, a subtree, and a new demo missing). Fix the tree, or gate it?
decisions.commitment: Both. Every docs/*.md, the docs/dogfood/ subtree, CHANGELOG.md, bench/retrieval_quality.py and demo/the_dogfooding.py were added to the tree, and tests/test_docs.py gained test_the_project_layout_lists_every_doc_and_no_ghosts — every docs/*.md must appear in the layout block, symmetric with the nestor/*.py gate, no-ghosts included. Proven to fail by removing a doc's line. Editing the gated test went through demo/review_desk.py first, as hooks/before_write.py requires.
decisions.why: A doc absent from the layout reads as nonexistent to anyone grepping the tree for what to read next — the exact small-model failure §8 named. Fixing the tree without gating it would have left the same class free to recur a third time; the package tree proves the gate is what keeps a layout honest, not diligence. The gate lives in the half of the tree that had none.

decisions.question: The standup found nestor calibrate still recommends a threshold from a corpus too small to mean anything, with no floor in the command's OWN output (only in README prose two sections away). Fix it in this pass?
decisions.commitment: First no, then yes. It was filed as IDEAS.md §6.95 open and left out of the docs pass; when the operator asked for the code change it shipped in this same branch, with the discipline a code change owes. STABLE_SAMPLE_FLOOR = 30 in nestor.calibrate; summarize() annotates the recommendation as '←recommended (unstable — too few pairs)' and prints an '!' caution when sampled is below the floor. The recommended number is unchanged — only the honesty around it moved to where a parser reads. tests/test_calibrate.py carries two tests that both fail on the unfixed revision (no STABLE_SAMPLE_FLOOR, no caution), and the claim is about the rule, so the second confirms the caution vanishes above the floor.
decisions.why: The reason to defer was real — a code change smuggled into a docs pass gets none of the discipline the agent-guide requires, and a docs refresh cannot see the edges of serving-adjacent output. The reason to ship anyway was the operator asking, which is authority a machine may act on (docs/agent-guide.md: chat is authority, even though it is not evidence). Shipping it with a recorded split and an unchanged recommendation keeps the deferral's caution — the change is narrow, tested against the unfixed revision, and touches only the output, not the number.

decisions.question: docs/releasing.md quotes 597 passed / 7 skipped, stale against today's 937/19. Update the number?
decisions.commitment: No. That figure is an explicitly dated hand-run snapshot (2026-08-06, four interpreters). It was left as written, with a visible parenthetical noting the suite has since grown to 937/19 on 3.11.
decisions.why: docs/agent-guide.md says to correct a wrong entry in place, visibly — a claim that was acted on is part of the record. Overwriting a dated measurement with a newer number falsifies what was true on the day it was taken; annotating it keeps both the record and the current truth.
